analysis.one_liner: Conditions federal airport grants on paying airport service workers at least $15 an hour with benefits.
analysis.headline: The bill attracted 97 House Democratic cosponsors but never received a committee vote, a hearing, or floor action, and died when the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required small, medium, and large hub airports to certify — as a condition of receiving federal airport improvement grants, terminal grants, infrastructure law money, and passenger facility charges — that service workers like baggage handlers, security officers, cleaners, and food and retail staff are paid at least $15 an hour or the higher local prevailing wage, with fringe benefits. Airports that did not certify would have been cut off from that federal funding. The Labor Department would set wage rates by job category. The bill was introduced, referred to committee, and never acted on again.
analysis.who_benefits: Airport service workers — security officers, baggage and ramp handlers, cleaners, ticketing agents, food service and retail workers at the nation's hub airports — would gain a federally enforced wage and benefits floor wherever their airport wanted federal grant money. Passengers would benefit indirectly from a more stable, better-trained workforce; the bill's own findings tie worker turnover to safety and security performance.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Airport service workers like cleaners and baggage handlers

how_it_helps.text: The bill bars the Transportation Secretary from approving airport development grants at small, medium, and large hub airports unless the airport certifies that all covered service workers are paid no less than the highest of $15 an hour, the federal contract minimum wage, or the applicable state or local minimum wage [S3].

Covered workers must also receive fringe benefits no less than the greater of Service Contract Act local determinations or applicable state or local requirements, and the certification must cover workers even when they are employed through contractors or subcontractors [S3].

The wage condition would attach not only to Airport Improvement Program grants but also to grants under the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act (airport infrastructure grants and the airport terminal program) and to approval to collect passenger facility charges, extending it to most federal money flowing to hub airports [S3].
The bill's findings state that a stable, well-paid airport workforce is critical to public safety and security and that reducing workforce turnover requires living wages and health coverage [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Airports, and the contractors and concession companies they hire — airlines' ground-handling firms, janitorial and security contractors, food and retail concessionaires — would bear higher payroll and benefits costs, and would risk losing federal grants and passenger facility charge authority if they did not comply. Travelers could eventually see some of those costs passed through concession prices or airport finances.

drawbacks.text: Conditioning federal grants on wage certification could slow or reduce airport infrastructure spending in places where operators resist the labor costs, meaning some needed safety and capacity projects could be delayed or underfunded [S3].

Higher labor costs at hub airports would be borne by airport operators and by contractors and concessionaires, who could pass some of it to travelers through higher concession prices or pass it to workers through reduced hiring or hours; the bill relies on annual certifications by employers, which is a self-reported compliance mechanism [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the hundreds of thousands of workers at hub airports, a firm wage and benefits floor tied to federal funding is a substantial gain, and the cost falls on a narrow set of airport-linked businesses rather than taxpayers. The main honest objection is the compliance mechanism — annual self-certification with discretionary enforcement — and the risk that some airport projects stall where operators balk. On balance the trade favors workers, and it died without ever being tested in debate.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Transportation and Infrastructure Committee, which sent it to its Aviation Subcommittee, and no further action — no hearing, markup, or vote — was ever taken before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Jesus 'Chuy' Garcia of Illinois introduced the Good Jobs for Good Airports Act on March 9, 2023 [S5].
The House referred it to the Transportation and Infrastructure Committee the day it was introduced, and to the committee's Aviation Subcommittee the next day [S5].
Ninety-seven House Democrats cosponsored the bill; no Republicans did [S4].
The action history shows no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action at any point before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Airports, airline ground-handling companies, and service and concession contractors that pay airport workers below $15 an hour with few benefits — they kept federal airport funding with no wage conditions attached, while the workers the bill covered got nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Airports and service contractors that kept funding with no wage floor

sides.party_line_note: All 97 cosponsors were House Democrats, and no Republican signed on, so the bill's support was entirely one-sided even before it stalled in committee.

industries.note: These companies employ most covered workers and would have had to raise pay and add benefits to keep their airport clients eligible for federal grants. Their interest in avoiding that cost ran directly against the workers' wage gain, which was the bill's whole point.

Hub airports would have faced higher labor costs at tenant employers and could have lost access to Airport Improvement Program grants, terminal grants, infrastructure-law money, and passenger facility charge authority for noncompliance. Airports already depend heavily on federal grants, so the condition would have real leverage.

Ramp agents, baggage handlers, and aircraft cleaners are explicitly covered, including workers employed through subcontractors, so airlines' outsourced ground operations would have borne the wage mandate.

industries.industry: Airport food service and retail concessionaires
industries.note: Concession workers at hubs are covered workers; food, beverage, retail, and lounge operators would have had to meet the wage and benefits floor. Airlines would benefit indirectly from a more stable, lower-turnover workforce but would pay through their contractors.
